questions.sampleAnswer: State sovereignty is the ability of a nation state to make laws for its citizens without external interference. The relationship between state sovereignty and human rights influences whether there is recognition, protection or enforcement of such rights. For example, a sovereign state may recognise the fundamental human rights as listed in an international instrument (eg ICCPR) and then enact them into domestic legislation. Conversely, a sovereign state may refuse to cooperate with an international instrument, or organisation such as the United Nations, as such rights may not reflect the values of that nation state.

questions.sampleAnswer: A number of important human rights have been protected in Australia, although their enforceability varies. For instance, there are explicit rights contained in the Australian Constitution such as the right to vote in Commonwealth elections (s. 41). Similarly, statute law has contributed to the enforcement of human rights through the application of legislation such as the Sex Discrimination Act 1984 (Cth). Common law also reveals how Australia responds and enforces human rights, such as Dietrich v The Queen 1992. The High Court of Australia recognised the importance of a fair trial if the accused represents themselves or has an unqualified person representing them. This right, however, does not automatically allow the accused to acquire legal assistance if they did not meet the criteria for legal aid. The Australian Human Rights Commission (AHRC) was establised by the AHRC Act 1986 (Cth). However, this legislation, while establishing the statutory authority, may not lead to binding or enforceable judgements. Some Australian responses to the implementation of international law can also limit the enforcement of human rights. This can be seen with Australia’s interpretation of the Refugee Convention 1951 (UN) through the Migration Act 1958 (Cth).

questions.sampleAnswer: The Australian Constitution, established in 1901, provides a framework to reflect changing values and ethical standards through judicial interpretation, referendums and legislative reforms. The few explicit rights identified in the Constitution, such as the right to freedom of religion (Section 116) arguably leave gaps in protection. Further, the Constitution does not list what the Australian values are. Due to the complexity of the process, Constitutional reform is not often accomplished, for example the 1988 Rights and Freedoms referendum which aimed at enshrining civil rights failed. Conversely, the Constitution does allow the High Court to uphold implied rights and adapt to changing values. This occurred in the 1997 case, Lange v Australia Broadcasting Corporation, which upheld the existence of freedom of political communication. Additionally, the Constitution provides a framework to reflect changing values and ethical standards, however, has limitations due to the complexity of the reform progress.

questions.sampleAnswer: State sovereignty influences whether there is recognition, protection or enforcement of human rights, such as the right to be free from slavery. Positively, nation states can use their right to govern themselves without external interference to ratify and enact international laws that uphold human rights. For example, Australia ratified the 2000 Palermo Protocol by amending D. 270 of the Criminal Code 2005 (Cth) to criminalise slavery practices including servitude, forced labour and deceptive recruiting for labour or services. An example of enforcement is the case of R v Wei Tang 2008 HCA which was Australia’s first conviction under this amendment. On the other hand, sovereignty allows states to infringe upon the human rights of its citizens. For example, North Korea had the highest rate of people experiencing modern slavery in 2023. Due to state sovereignty, the international community is unable to interfere with global failures to uphold the right to be free from slavery.
